A1.justification: Both PDFs describe video-SALMONN S, with a shared streaming-memory framework and overlapping evaluations. All pages, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable. The substantial method and protocol revisions limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent reliable document comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component and optimizer ablations, memory-size experiments and inference analyses, including results in Appendices A-C.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, ELViM dataset analyses, component ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative experiments, including Appendices A-G.

M1.justification: v1's Hessian-free, conjugate-gradient TTT module becomes TTTMEM with an additional delayed-input prediction loss and one-step SGD updates. v2 adds two-stage training that freezes TTT parameters during the second stage, switches from Qwen2.5-VL to Qwen3-VL, and replaces the reader's selection procedure with recurrent, modality-masked KV selection that preserves interleaved text tokens.

E1.justification: v2 introduces ELViM, testing procedural recall after at least 30 minutes of intervening videos, and evaluates real-time, omni-modal and contextual tasks on StreamingBench. MLVU and the OVO-Bench evaluation in v1 Appendix B disappear. Video-MME, LVBench and VideoEvalPro remain, as do the named training-data sources.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated PEMF and K-means clustering comparators and replaces Qwen2.5-VL comparisons with Qwen3-VL-based comparisons. Evaluations of Video-LLaMA-3, Dispider, StreamMem, TTTMuon and LaCT disappear. Standard TTT, Mamba-2 and merging/discarding comparisons persist. AdaReTaKe changes from an enhancement of the non-streaming baseline to a competing reader applied to video-SALMONN S.

E3.justification: The backbone changes from Qwen2.5-VL 7B to Qwen3-VL 8B, and the audio-visual LLaVA training subset increases from about 13k to 100k videos. v2 adds a training epoch with a 2048-frame cap after the 1024-frame stage. Its main reading setup uses 32k stored tokens with 8k chunks instead of v1's 128k. It also standardizes comparison backbones/data and introduces delayed-replay, partial-video and runtime evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds ablations of long-span prediction, second-stage training, deepstack placement and prediction span, plus temporal-distance analysis and open-ended ELViM case studies. Memory-size and frame-count sweeps are retained but redesigned. v1's curvature/CG convergence study and Muon-versus-HF information-flow analysis are removed, including their appendix evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports actual seed/run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or a specified significance-testing procedure. v1's promise to release seeds is not a report of experimental repetitions. v2's dataset and runtime statistics do not introduce repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main audio-visual reading model reports Video-MME overall/long accuracies of 74.2/67.8 in v1 and 76.9/71.3 in v2. These are replacement results under changed backbones, training and memory settings, not an isolated same-setting gain. v2 adds ELViM results, including 46.7% versus 32.5% for video-SALMONN 2+, and extensive new ablation/runtime results; MLVU, OVO-Bench and optimizer-comparison results disappear.

T1.justification: v1's second-order/HF derivation, curvature-matrix definitions, token-weighted loss formulation and CG stopping reasoning in Section 3.2 and Appendix A are removed. v2 formally defines the delayed-input prediction objective and a different masked, recurrent KV-selection rule in Sections 3.1 and 3.3. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: Both retain the claim of fixed-memory processing beyond three hours at 1 FPS and 360p. However, v2 replaces the central HF-optimization contribution with long-span prediction, two-stage training and modality-aware reading. It adds a benchmark contribution and claims about acquiring procedural knowledge from past video experiences, replacing v1's Video-MME-centered headline with broader memory-learning claims.

C2.justification: v1 explains performance through HF's balance between reconstruction convergence and information flow. v2 instead emphasizes temporal regularization, sparse-sampling failures and recent-memory bias, supported by new case studies. It qualifies retention as preserving useful summaries and discusses prediction-span noise, deepstack overhead and memory-dependent saturation. The impact discussion also adds concerns specific to persistent memory, including privacy and forgetting.

D1.justification: v2 documents TTT layer dimensions, prediction-span settings, deepstack handling, per-GPU batch size, second-stage training time and ELViM collection/filtering/annotation procedures. v1's detailed HF/CG and Muon implementation guidance disappears. Whereas v1 promises future releases, v2 supplies a repository link and states that implementation code and ELViM questions accompany supplementary material; actual external availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from Hessian-free optimization to episodic procedural memory. v2 removes the associated HF/Muon literature, distinguishes its use of TTT from prior video-stream segmentation work, and contrasts ELViM with VideoMMMU. New references include Qwen3-VL, StreamForest, Cambrian-S and StreamingBench, supporting a substantially revised novelty and evaluation context.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The methodology and experimental narrative are reorganized around TTTMEM, two-stage training and a dedicated ELViM section. The appendices are restructured, and separate ethics/reproducibility sections become an impact statement and dispersed access disclosures.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from single-column to two-column layout, redraws the architecture and TTT diagrams, and adds training and benchmark-construction diagrams. It replaces optimizer plots with revised memory/frame plots and temporal-distance analysis, adds illustrated examples and case studies, and substantially restructures the benchmark and ablation tables.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for useful long-term memory through a targeted delayed-recall benchmark, more consistently controlled streaming comparisons, temporal-retention ablations and measured runtime/memory costs. These address important gaps in v1's predominantly general-video and optimizer-focused evidence. The gains outweigh narrower retained benchmark coverage and reporting weaknesses, including ELViM merging accuracy of 38.5% in Table 1 versus 35.4% in Table 2 and the abstract's 15-point claim versus the table-supported 14.2 points. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and higher cross-version scores alone do not establish improvement.
